title: Essay Writing & Argumentation
description: Structuring arguments clearly — thesis statements, PEEL paragraphs, using evidence, persuasive techniques, and the writing process from planning to editing.

notes.heading: The Thesis Statement
notes.body: A thesis statement is the central argument of your essay — one clear, specific, debatable sentence telling the reader exactly what you will argue. It appears at the end of your introduction. A strong thesis: takes a stance (not just states a fact), is specific and focused, can be supported with evidence, and previews the essay's structure. Weak: 'Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet is about love.' Strong: 'Shakespeare presents love in Romeo and Juliet as an impulsive, destructive force that leads to tragedy, challenging the romantic idealisation of young love.' Your thesis is a promise — everything that follows must support it.

illustration.alt: Diagram of essay structure showing an introduction ending with a highlighted thesis statement, three PEEL body paragraphs (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link), and a conclusion.
illustration.caption: The thesis sits at the end of the introduction, and every PEEL body paragraph must support it.

notes.heading: Essay Structure
notes.body: Introduction: Hook the reader → provide context/background → state your thesis. Keep it concise (3-5 sentences). Body paragraphs: Each develops ONE main point supporting your thesis using PEEL structure. Order logically (chronological, by importance, compare/contrast). Conclusion: Restate thesis in new words, synthesise key points (don't just list them), end with broader significance — 'so what?' Avoid 'In conclusion...' — transition naturally: 'Ultimately,' 'Through this analysis,' 'As demonstrated.' Common mistakes: too many points per paragraph, paragraphs that don't link to thesis, conclusions introducing new arguments, summarising instead of analysing.

notes.heading: PEEL Paragraph Method
notes.body: PEEL is the gold standard for academic paragraphs. (P) Point — topic sentence stating the main idea. Must link to thesis. (E) Evidence — quotation, statistic, or example. Integrate smoothly — don't 'plonk' quotes. (E) Explanation — the most important part. Analyse HOW evidence proves your point. What techniques are used? Why did the author choose these words? (L) Link — connect back to thesis and/or transition to next paragraph. Example: P: 'The author uses dark imagery to establish a foreboding atmosphere.' E: 'The 'blood-red sun sank beneath the jagged horizon.' E: 'The colour symbolism of 'blood-red' foreshadows violence, while 'jagged' connotes danger and pain, preparing the reader for...' L: 'This ominous opening establishes the tragic tone that pervades the novel.'

notes.heading: Using Evidence and Embedding Quotations
notes.body: Evidence types: direct quotations, paraphrasing, specific examples, statistics, expert opinions. Embedding quotations: integrate into your own sentence. Bad: 'The character is sad. 'I feel so alone,' he said.' Good: 'The character's isolation is palpable when he confesses he feels 'so alone,' revealing the depth of his despair.' Short quotations (1-2 words) can be the most powerful — embed seamlessly. Use ellipsis (...) to omit words. Use brackets [ ] to clarify. Citing: MYP requires consistent referencing — author surname + page (Orwell 42). Analysis must follow evidence — never end a paragraph with a quotation.

notes.heading: Rhetorical and Persuasive Techniques
notes.body: Persuasive writing uses specific techniques: Ethos (credibility/authority), Pathos (emotion — fear, pity, hope), Logos (logic — facts, statistics). Rhetorical questions — asked for effect, not answers. 'How long must we wait for justice?' Repetition/anaphora — repeating words/phrases for emphasis: 'We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds...' (Churchill). Tricolon (rule of three) — three elements for rhythm: 'Government of the people, by the people, for the people' (Lincoln). Hyperbole — deliberate exaggeration. Anecdote — brief personal story to humanise an argument. Counter-argument — acknowledging opposing views then refuting them (strengthens your position by showing balanced thinking).

notes.heading: Analytical Writing vs Summary
notes.body: The most common essay mistake: summarising instead of analysing. Summary tells WHAT: 'Macbeth kills King Duncan.' Analysis explains WHY and HOW: 'Macbeth's murder of Duncan represents his moral descent, catalysed by unchecked ambition and Lady Macbeth's manipulation. Shakespeare uses blood symbolism ('Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand?') to convey Macbeth's irreversible guilt.' Analysis involves: identifying techniques (symbolism, metaphor, structure), explaining effects on readers, linking to themes, exploring multiple interpretations. Signal phrases: 'This suggests...' 'The author's use of... implies...' 'This reveals...' Never repeat 'This shows that...' — vary your analytical vocabulary.

notes.heading: Planning, Drafting and Editing
notes.body: Writing process: (1) Unpack the question — identify command words (analyse, evaluate, compare), topic, and scope. (2) Brainstorm — mind map, list ideas. (3) Plan — outline thesis, 3-4 main points, evidence for each. A 5-minute plan saves 30 minutes of rewriting. (4) Draft quickly — don't edit while drafting. (5) Revise — check structure, argument coherence, evidence integration. Read aloud to catch awkward phrasing. (6) Edit — grammar, spelling, punctuation. (7) Proofread after a break. Editing checklist: Does every paragraph support the thesis? Is each quotation analysed? Have you varied sentence structure? Is the conclusion more than a summary?

flashcards.definition: A clear, debatable, specific sentence stating your essay's central argument. Appears at end of introduction.
flashcards.example: 'Orwell's Animal Farm critiques totalitarianism by demonstrating how revolutionary ideals are corrupted by power.'

flashcards.definition: Point → Evidence → Explanation → Link. Each body paragraph develops one main idea.
flashcards.example: P: claim. E: quote. E: analyse. L: connect to thesis/next paragraph.

flashcards.definition: First sentence of a body paragraph stating its main point. Must link to the thesis.
flashcards.example: 'The author uses pathetic fallacy to mirror the protagonist's emotional turmoil.'

flashcards.definition: Integrating a quote into your own sentence rather than dropping it standalone.
flashcards.example: Bad: 'He was angry. 'I will not tolerate this.'' Good: 'His anger surfaces when he declares he 'will not tolerate this.''

flashcards.definition: Modes of persuasion: Ethos=credibility, Pathos=emotion, Logos=logic/facts.
flashcards.example: Ethos: 'As a doctor...' Pathos: 'Imagine your child...' Logos: 'Statistics show...'

flashcards.definition: A question asked for persuasive effect, not for an answer. Engages the reader.
flashcards.example: 'If not now, when? If not us, who?'

flashcards.definition: Three parallel elements in succession for rhythmic, memorable impact.
flashcards.example: 'Veni, vidi, vici.' 'Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.'

flashcards.definition: Acknowledging an opposing viewpoint then refuting it — strengthens your position.
flashcards.example: 'Some may argue... However, this overlooks the evidence that...'

flashcards.definition: Repetition of a word/phrase at the beginning of successive clauses for emphasis.
flashcards.example: 'I have a dream... I have a dream... I have a dream...' (MLK).

flashcards.definition: Summary = what happens. Analysis = why/how it matters, what techniques are used, what effects are created.
flashcards.example: Summary: 'Temperature dropped.' Analysis: 'The sudden temperature drop mirrors the protagonist's emotional withdrawal, using pathetic fallacy.'

flashcards.definition: Words/phrases connecting ideas: however, furthermore, consequently, in contrast, similarly, therefore.
flashcards.example: 'The author initially portrays the character as heroic. However, this impression is undermined when...'

flashcards.definition: A short personal story used to illustrate a point and create emotional connection.
flashcards.example: 'Last week, I met a single mother working three jobs just to afford childcare...'
